--- title: "Seurat workflow: PBMC" author: "Wiktor Mikolajczak" editor: visual --- # Note This vignette is based on [Seurat - Guided clustering tutorial](https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/pbmc3k_tutorial) Use this vignette as a general guideline, not a ground truth. There is no one way to analyze genomics data. Sometimes you have to adjust your analysis based on your research question, experimental design etc. In the future you will analyze genomic data that you or other people generated. It is vital that, before any analysis, you familiarize yourself with the data set: - What is the biological question you are trying to answer? What are the hypotheses? - What is the study design and how was the experiment done (sample type, treatment, genetic knockout, disease, sample size, system, technology, are there any batches etc.)? - How was the data processed (software, genome version etc.)? - What type of data are available (raw data, count matrices, sample/cell metadata)? Instead of just copy-pasting the code, try implementing the following logic: 1. Read the vignette first. Try to understand each step. 2. Without looking at the vignette, write down the main steps of the workflow (use headers to build an outline of your document at the same time). For each step, write a short comment: What is this step for?, Why is it important? Compare your answers with the vignette. It is ok if you don't remember the exact code or the name of the functions. It's more important that you understand each step conceptually. 3. After each step write down your observations. What has changed? 4. At the end of your analysis, think about and write down conclusions. It doesn't have to be an academic assay but try to state the main points and do a little bit of goggling. - Are you able to answer the initial research question and confirm/deny the hypotheses? - Try to connect what is known with what you have found. The goal of this training is to help you understand the general workflow of single-cell RNA-seq analysis. Although using AI can be beneficial and speed up your analysis, it is important that you have a good understanding of topics covered in this training and you have truly mastered the skill. Only then you can use AI to help you with the analysis. It is fine, to ask AI to help you with customizing a ggplot, but try not to use it for the actual analysis. If you don't know what a function does, run `?function_name` in Console. # About the dataset For this tutorial, we will be analyzing a dataset of Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMC) freely available from 10X Genomics. There are 2,700 single cells that were sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 500. The raw data can be found [here](https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell/pbmc3k/pbmc3k_filtered_gene_bc_matrices.tar.gz). PBMCs are blood cells with a round nucleus: mostly T cells, plus B cells, NK cells and monocytes (and a small number of dendritic cells and platelets). They are easy to collect from a blood draw, which makes them a popular sample for benchmarking and for learning single-cell RNA-seq. This dataset ("PBMC 3k") comes from a single healthy human donor and was generated with the 10X Genomics Chromium platform. The data were processed with cellranger and aligned to the human reference genome (hg19). Because there is only one sample, there are no treatment groups or batches to compare. Our goal is to identify the cell types present in the sample, based on clustering and marker gene expression. The data can be also found on [my github](https://github.com/wiktormiko/Intro-to-genomics/tree/main/vignettes/data/pbmc/filtered_gene_bc_matrices/hg19) ## Structure of the cellranger output The downloaded archive contains a folder (`filtered_gene_bc_matrices/hg19/`) with three files. Together they describe one count matrix, split into the matrix itself and the labels for its rows and columns: - `barcodes.tsv`: one cell barcode per line (e.g. `AAACATACAACCAC-1`). Each barcode is a short DNA sequence that tags all reads from one droplet, so it identifies one cell. The suffix `-1` is the GEM well (sample) number. These are the **columns** of the matrix (2,700 lines here). Only barcodes that cellranger called as cells are included, empty droplets are removed ("filtered" matrix). - `genes.tsv`: one gene per line, with two tab-separated columns: the Ensembl gene ID (e.g. `ENSG00000243485`) and the gene symbol (e.g. `MIR1302-10`). These are the **rows** of the matrix, one for every gene in the reference annotation (32,738 for hg19), whether or not it was detected. In newer cellranger versions this file is called `features.tsv.gz` and has a third column giving the feature type (e.g. `Gene Expression`). - `matrix.mtx`: the UMI counts, stored in the sparse format. Most entries in a single-cell matrix are zero (a cell expresses only a fraction of all genes), so only non-zero values are stored. After the header lines, there is a line with the total number of rows, columns and non-zero entries, followed by one line per non-zero entry with three numbers: `gene_index cell_index count`. The indices point to the line numbers in `genes.tsv` and `barcodes.tsv`. For example, `1234 5 3` means that the gene on line 1234 of `genes.tsv` has 3 UMIs in the cell on line 5 of `barcodes.tsv`. `Read10X()` reads these three files and combines them into a single sparse matrix (a `dgCMatrix`) with genes as row names and barcodes as column names. That format is very similar to bulk RNA-seq data, where rows represent genes and columns represent samples. In single-cell we have cells/barcodes instead of samples. ## What is a UMI? A UMI (Unique Molecular Identifier) is a short random DNA sequence added to each individual mRNA molecule during reverse transcription, before the cDNA is amplified by PCR. Amplification produces many copies of the same molecule, so counting reads would overestimate highly amplified molecules. Reads from the same cell and gene that carry the same UMI are copies of one original molecule, so they are collapsed and counted once. This is why the values in the matrix are the number of mRNA molecules detected, not the number of reads. ## How is this different from bulk RNA-seq? Bulk RNA-seq measures RNA from thousands to millions of cells pooled together, so each gene has one value per sample: an average over all cells. Single-cell RNA-seq keeps the cells separate, so each gene has one value per cell. This lets us find cell types and states that would be hidden in the average, for example in PBMCs, where T cells, B cells and monocytes are mixed together. The data look different too, and this affects the analysis: - **Size:** a bulk experiment has a handful of samples (columns), a single-cell experiment has thousands of cells. - **Sparsity:** each cell contains very little RNA (a few pg) and only a fraction of it is captured, so most entries in the matrix are zero. Some zeros are true absence of expression, others are "dropouts" where a molecule was missed. Bulk data have far fewer zeros. - **Counts:** in bulk RNA-seq, reads are usually counted directly (full-length protocols, no UMIs). Because single-cell protocols need a lot of PCR amplification from tiny amounts of RNA, UMIs are used to remove amplification bias. - **Noise:** gene expression is noisy at the single-cell level (both biological and technical), so we need cell-level quality control (e.g. number of genes, mitochondrial content) and dimensionality reduction before clustering. - **Question:** bulk RNA-seq compares conditions (differential expression between samples), single-cell RNA-seq is often used (but not only) to discover and annotate cell populations. [**How does single cell RNA-seq work**](https://www.10xgenomics.com/blog/how-does-single-cell-rna-seq-work) # Saving your work Some steps in this workflow (normalization, PCA, clustering, UMAP) take time, and the results can change slightly if you rerun them with a different seed or settings. After an important step, save the Seurat object to disk with `saveRDS()`, and load it later with `readRDS()`, so you don't have to rerun everything. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Save the object (after clustering, for example) saveRDS(pbmc, file = "data/pbmc_clustered.rds") # Load it in a new session pbmc <- readRDS("data/pbmc_clustered.rds") ``` ::: Tips: - The `.rds` file stores one R object with everything in it: counts, normalized data, metadata, PCA, UMAP and clusters. - Save versions at different steps (e.g. `pbmc_qc.rds`, `pbmc_clustered.rds`, `pbmc_annotated.rds`) instead of overwriting one file, so you can go back to an earlier step. - Seurat objects can be large, so don't commit them to git (add them to `.gitignore`) and avoid storing them in synced folders if you can. - The object is tied to the Seurat version it was created with, so note the version (`packageVersion("Seurat")`) and, if needed, update the object with `UpdateSeuratObject()` after loading it in a newer one. - `saveRDS()` saves one object. To save several objects, use `save()` and `load()`, or save them in a list. # Libraries ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Install these packages if you haven't already # install.packages("Seurat") # devtools::install_github("immunogenomics/presto") ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(patchwork) library(Seurat) library(clustree) ``` ::: # Seurat object ## Set up Seurat object We start by reading in the data. The [`Read10X()`](https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/read10x) function reads in the output of the [cellranger](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/cell-ranger/latest/getting-started/cr-what-is-cell-ranger) pipeline from 10X, returning a unique molecular identified (UMI) count matrix. The values in this matrix represent the number of molecules for each feature (i.e. gene; row) that are detected in each cell (column). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc_data <- Read10X("data/pbmc/filtered_gene_bc_matrices/hg19/") # Create a seurat object pbmc <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = pbmc_data, project = 'pbmc', min.cells = 10, min.features = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Feature names cannot have underscores ('_'), replacing with dashes ('-') ``` ::: ::: `min.cells`: Include features detected in at least this many cells. We can already set up small cutoffs to filter out cells or genes. This is an arbitrary threshold that should be used carefully and customized depending on the dataset. `min.cells = 10` is reasonable for this dataset, and it's a common choice. With 2,700 cells, 10 cells is about 0.4% of the data. Genes seen in fewer cells than that are mostly noise and add little to clustering. The cost is rare populations. If a cell type makes up less than about 0.4% of the cells (roughly 10 cells here), a marker gene specific to it could be filtered out. If you are unsure what to do, or expect to identify rare cell types, it's better to not set any thresholds. `min.features`: Include cells where at least this many features are detected. It's better to leave it at 0, because we will perform a separate QC and cell filtering. ## Seurat object structure ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2700 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 0 variable features) 1 layer present: counts ``` ::: ::: The printed summary tells us that the object has 2,700 cells (called "samples" here), a number of genes (features) that passed `min.cells`, and one assay called `RNA`. The object has no variable features yet and only one layer (`counts`), because we haven't done any analysis. A Seurat object is an S4 object, a container with several slots. Each slot stores a different piece of the analysis, so everything about one dataset stays together and in sync. You can list the slots with `slotNames()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} slotNames(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "assays" "meta.data" "active.assay" "active.ident" "graphs" [6] "neighbors" "reductions" "images" "project.name" "misc" [11] "version" "commands" "tools" ``` ::: ::: The most important ones are: - `assays`: the expression data (counts, normalized data, scaled data). - `meta.data`: a data frame with one row per cell, for cell-level information. - `active.ident`: the cell identity (cluster or cell type) used by default for plotting and DE. - `reductions`: dimensionality reductions (PCA, UMAP). - `graphs` and `neighbors`: the nearest-neighbor graphs used for clustering. - `commands`: a log of the Seurat functions that were run on the object and their parameters. Right now `reductions` and `graphs` are empty. They will be filled in as we go. ### Assays and layers An assay holds the expression matrices for one type of measurement. Our data have a single assay, `RNA`, but one object can have more (e.g. `ADT` for surface proteins, or `SCT` after SCTransform). `DefaultAssay()` tells us which assay is used when we don't specify one. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Assays(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "RNA" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} DefaultAssay(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "RNA" ``` ::: ::: In Seurat v5, each assay stores its matrices in *layers*. At the moment there is just `counts`, the raw UMI counts. After normalization and scaling we will also get `data` (log-normalized values) and `scale.data` (scaled values used for PCA). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Layers(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "counts" ``` ::: ::: Let's look at the counts layer. It is the sparse matrix we read in with `Read10X()` (genes in rows, cells in columns), filtered by `min.cells`. The dots are zeros. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc[["RNA"]]$counts[1:5, 1:3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5 x 3 sparse Matrix of class "dgCMatrix" AAACATACAACCAC-1 AAACATTGAGCTAC-1 AAACATTGATCAGC-1 LINC00115 . . . NOC2L . . . HES4 . . . ISG15 . . 1 C1orf159 . . . ``` ::: ::: ### Cell metadata `meta.data` has one row per cell (the row names are the barcodes). Seurat adds a few columns automatically: - `orig.ident`: the sample name (the `project` we set). - `nCount_RNA`: the number of UMIs in the cell. - `nFeature_RNA`: the number of genes detected in the cell. The concept of `meta.data` in single-cell is the same as in bulk RNA-seq and DESeq2 workflow. Instead of biological samples, the row represents cells/barcodes. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(pbmc@meta.data) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # or # head(pbmc[[]]) ``` ::: We will add more columns here later, such as the percentage of mitochondrial genes and the cluster. Metadata columns can be accessed with `$`, e.g. `pbmc$nCount_RNA`. If we have more samples, conditions or batches, this is where we store that information. ### Identities Every cell also has an identity. By default it is the `orig.ident`, and later it will be the cluster. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(Idents(pbmc)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AAACATACAACCAC-1 AAACATTGAGCTAC-1 AAACATTGATCAGC-1 AAACCGTGCTTCCG-1 pbmc pbmc pbmc pbmc AAACCGTGTATGCG-1 AAACGCACTGGTAC-1 pbmc pbmc Levels: pbmc ``` ::: ::: ### Useful accessors Prefer these functions to digging into slots with `@`, because they work across Seurat versions. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(pbmc) # genes x cells ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11139 2700 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(rownames(pbmc)) # gene names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "LINC00115" "NOC2L" "HES4" "ISG15" "C1orf159" "TNFRSF18" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(colnames(pbmc)) # cell barcodes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "AAACATACAACCAC-1" "AAACATTGAGCTAC-1" "AAACATTGATCAGC-1" "AAACCGTGCTTCCG-1" [5] "AAACCGTGTATGCG-1" "AAACGCACTGGTAC-1" ``` ::: ::: | What | How | |---------------------|-------------------------------------------| | Counts matrix | `pbmc[["RNA"]]$counts` | | One metadata column | `pbmc$nCount_RNA` | | All metadata | `pbmc@meta.data` or `pbmc[[]]` | | Cell identities | `Idents(pbmc)` | | Assays / layers | `Assays(pbmc)`, `Layers(pbmc)` | | Reductions | `Reductions(pbmc)` | | Subset the object | `subset(pbmc, subset = nCount_RNA > 500)` | As we run the workflow, come back to the object and check what has changed. # Initial processing ## QC and selecting cells for further analysis Similarly to the DESeq2 workflow - where we also did some QC's, e.g. remove low-count genes - we will do something similar. Instead of filtering "low quality genes", we will remove "low quality **cells**". Low-quality cells (dying or damaged cells, empty droplets, doublets) have unreliable or misleading expression profiles, so if you leave them in, they add noise, form artificial clusters, and distort normalization and downstream results like clustering and differential expression. Here are some of the [commonly used metrics for QC checks](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758103/): - The number of unique genes detected in each cell. - Low-quality cells or empty droplets will often have very few genes - Cell doublets or multiplets may exhibit an aberrantly high gene count - Similarly, the total number of molecules detected within a cell (correlates strongly with unique genes) - The percentage of reads that map to the mitochondrial genome - Low-quality / dying cells often exhibit extensive mitochondrial contamination - We calculate mitochondrial QC metrics with the [`PercentageFeatureSet()`](https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/percentagefeatureset) function, which calculates the percentage of counts originating from a set of features - We use the set of all genes starting with `MT-` as a set of mitochondrial genes (`mt-` in mouse) The number of unique genes (**`nFeature_RNA`**) in each cell and total number of UMI (**`nCount_RNA`**) in each cell are already present in the meta.data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(pbmc[[]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: We have to calculate the percentage of mitochondrial genes in each cell. That kind of information belongs to `meta.data`, so we will append this information as a new column. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc$percent.mt <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^MT-") # MT- for human, mt- for mouse ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(pbmc[[]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: There is now a new column in metadata, describing a percentage of mitochondrial genes in each cell. Visualizing these metrics will help us determine, what thresholds to use for filtering. Seurat has plenty of built-in plotting functions. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} VlnPlot(pbmc, features = c('nCount_RNA', 'nFeature_RNA', 'percent.mt')) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_pbmc_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=720} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} VlnPlot(pbmc, features = c('nCount_RNA', 'nFeature_RNA', 'percent.mt'), pt.size = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_pbmc_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-2.png){fig-align='center' width=720} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot1 <- FeatureScatter(pbmc, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt") plot2 <- FeatureScatter(pbmc, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA") plot1 + plot2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_pbmc_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### Rule of thumb for setting the cutoffs There are no universal thresholds. Use the violin plots to see where the bulk of the cells is and where the tails are, then cut off only the clear outliers. - Look at the shape of each distribution. Most cells form one main "body". Cells in a long tail, or in a separate small bump far from the body, are candidates for removal. Place the cutoff in the valley between the body and the tail, not inside the body. - Be conservative. It is easier to remove more cells later than to get back cells you have already filtered out. Filter, run the pipeline, and check whether the cells you removed or kept make sense. - Look at the metrics together, not one at a time. For example, `FeatureScatter()` of `nCount_RNA` vs `nFeature_RNA` or `percent.mt` shows whether cells with a high mitochondrial percentage also have low counts (low quality), or whether some cells have many counts and many genes (possible doublets). - Thresholds should be set per sample, because different samples and batches can have different distributions. - Write down the cutoffs you chose and why, and report how many cells were removed. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Example (adjust the values based on your plots) umi_lo <- 700 umi_hi <- 7000 ngenes_lo <- 250 ngenes_hi <- 2000 mito_lo <- 5 ``` ::: Before we remove any cells, let's add a new column to the metadata that says which cells have passed the filtering criteria ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc$QC_pass <- pbmc$nCount_RNA > umi_lo & pbmc$nCount_RNA < umi_hi & pbmc$nFeature_RNA > ngenes_lo & pbmc$nFeature_RNA < ngenes_hi & pbmc$percent.mt < mito_lo ``` ::: `QC_pass` is `TRUE` for cells that pass all the criteria and `FALSE` for cells that fail at least one. Let's see how many cells would be removed. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} table(pbmc$QC_pass) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` FALSE TRUE 104 2596 ``` ::: ::: I am going to write my own ggplot because I want more flexibility ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} qc_colors <- c("TRUE" = "grey70", "FALSE" = "red") thresholds <- tibble( metric = c("nCount_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA", "nFeature_RNA", "percent.mt"), value = c(umi_lo, umi_hi, ngenes_lo, ngenes_hi, mito_lo) ) p1 <- pbmc[[]] %>% select(QC_pass, nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA, percent.mt) %>% pivot_longer(-QC_pass, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>% arrange(QC_pass) %>% # FALSE cells are drawn last, on top ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) + geom_violin(fill = "grey95", color = "grey40") + geom_jitter(aes(color = QC_pass), width = 0.3, size = 0.3, alpha = .5) + geom_hline(data = thresholds, aes(yintercept = value), linetype = "dashed") + scale_color_manual(values = qc_colors) + facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = NULL) + theme_bw() p2 <- FeatureScatter(pbmc, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", group.by = 'QC_pass', pt.size = .2) + scale_color_manual(values = qc_colors) p3 <- FeatureScatter(pbmc, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA", group.by = 'QC_pass', pt.size = .2) + scale_color_manual(values = qc_colors) (p1 + (p2 + p3)) + plot_layout(nrow = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_pbmc_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1200} ::: ::: Once we are satisfied with our cutoffs, we can remove these low-quality cells. Remember that single-cell analysis is an iterative process and often times you need to go back to previous steps and adjust some parameters. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2700 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 0 variable features) 1 layer present: counts ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- subset(pbmc, subset = QC_pass) # keeps cells where QC_pass == TRUE # This is equivalent to: pbmc <- subset(pbmc, subset = QC_pass==TRUE) ``` ::: Always double check that what you removed worked properly ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2596 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 0 variable features) 1 layer present: counts ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(pbmc$QC_pass) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` TRUE 2596 ``` ::: ::: We successfully removed low quality cells (104) and we are left with 2596 cells. ## Data normalization Cells differ in how many UMIs we detect, even if they have the same amount of RNA, because of differences in capture efficiency and sequencing depth. If we compared raw counts, a cell with more UMIs would look like it expresses everything more highly. Normalization removes this technical difference so that cells can be compared. By default, Seurat uses `NormalizeData()` with the `LogNormalize` method: 1. Divide the counts of each gene in a cell by the total counts of that cell. 2. Multiply by a scale factor (10,000 by default). 3. Add 1 and take the natural log (`log1p`). The result is stored in the `data` layer, and the raw counts stay untouched in the `counts` layer. The log transform reduces the influence of very highly expressed genes, and makes the data closer to what PCA and clustering work best with. **How is it different from DESeq2?** - **What is normalized:** in DESeq2 the unit is a sample (a bulk library), and in Seurat it is a single cell. Seurat computes one size factor per cell (the total UMI count). - **Size factors:** DESeq2 uses the median-of-ratios method. It assumes that most genes are not differentially expressed, and it uses a geometric mean per gene across samples. This breaks down for single-cell data, because most genes have zero counts in at least one cell, which makes the geometric mean zero. Simple library-size scaling works better for sparse data. - **Purpose:** DESeq2 normalization is designed for comparing conditions between samples. Seurat normalization is mostly designed for comparing cells, in order to find structure (clusters) in the data. There are other approaches, for example `SCTransform()`, which models counts with regularized negative binomial regression and replaces `NormalizeData()`, `FindVariableFeatures()` and `ScaleData()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2596 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 0 variable features) 1 layer present: counts ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- NormalizeData(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Normalizing layer: counts ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2596 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 0 variable features) 2 layers present: counts, data ``` ::: ::: Notice that running normalization added a new layer `data` that stores normalized counts. ## Feature selection Not all of the \~11,000 genes are useful for finding cell populations. Most genes are either not expressed, or expressed at a similar level in all cells (e.g. housekeeping genes), so they mostly add noise. The genes that differ strongly between cells, called **highly variable genes (HVGs)**, are the ones that carry the information about cell types and states. Selecting HVGs for downstream analysis (PCA, clustering) has several advantages: - It focuses the analysis on the biological signal, which makes the cell populations easier to separate. - It reduces noise from lowly informative genes. - It makes the computation faster. Seurat's `FindVariableFeatures()` uses the `vst` method by default. You may recognize this approach from DESeq2: before calculating PCA we used vst and selected top 10% most variable genes. By default the top 2,000 genes are selected. The number is a convention, and results are usually robust to moderate changes (e.g. 1,000-3,000). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- FindVariableFeatures(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Finding variable features for layer counts ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2596 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 2000 variable features) 2 layers present: counts, data ``` ::: ::: The selected genes are stored in the object and can be accessed with `VariableFeatures()`. The [`ScaleData()`](https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/scaledata) function: - Shifts the expression of each gene, so that the mean expression across cells is 0 - Scales the expression of each gene, so that the variance across cells is 1 - This step gives equal weight in downstream analyses, so that highly-expressed genes do not dominate The results of this are stored in `pbmc[["RNA"]]$scale.data`. By default, only variable features are scaled; you can specify the `features` argument to scale additional features. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- ScaleData(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Centering and scaling data matrix ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2596 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 2000 variable features) 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data ``` ::: ::: ### Regressing out unwanted variation `ScaleData()` can also remove the effect of a variable that you don't want to drive the analysis, using the `vars.to.regress` argument. For each gene, Seurat fits a linear model of the (normalized) expression as a function of the variable, and keeps the residuals (what the variable cannot explain) as the scaled values. In other words, the part of the expression that is explained by the variable is subtracted. Typical variables to regress out are technical, such as `nCount_RNA` or `percent.mt`, or biological, such as the cell cycle phase. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Example: regress out the percentage of mitochondrial genes # Do not run pbmc <- ScaleData(pbmc, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt") ``` ::: Note that: - Regression only changes `scale.data` (used for PCA). The `counts` and `data` layers are not changed, so it does not affect plots of normalized expression or differential expression tests that use `data`. - Regress out only what you have a reason to. Regression can remove real biological signal if the variable is correlated with it (e.g. a high `percent.mt` can be a real property of a cell type), and it makes the results harder to interpret. - First check whether the variable is a problem. Run the analysis without regression and see if the cells separate by that variable (for example, in the PCA or UMAP colored by `percent.mt`). - Regression is not a replacement for batch correction between samples. ### Cell cycle scoring and regression Cells in different phases of the cell cycle express different genes (e.g. DNA replication genes in S phase, mitosis genes in G2/M). In proliferating tissues this can be a strong source of variation, and cells may cluster by cell cycle phase instead of by cell type. Seurat can score each cell with `CellCycleScoring()`, based on the expression of lists of S phase and G2/M phase marker genes (these are included in the package for human genes). The function adds `S.Score`, `G2M.Score` and `Phase` (G1, S or G2M) to the metadata. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} s.genes <- cc.genes.updated.2019$s.genes g2m.genes <- cc.genes.updated.2019$g2m.genes pbmc <- CellCycleScoring(pbmc, s.features = s.genes, g2m.features = g2m.genes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The following features are not present in the object: DTL, UHRF1, CENPU, RAD51AP1, CCNE2, CDC45, CDC6, EXO1, DSCC1, CASP8AP2, POLA1, E2F8, not searching for symbol synonyms ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The following features are not present in the object: CDK1, UBE2C, BIRC5, TPX2, TOP2A, NUF2, CENPF, PIMREG, CCNB2, CKAP2L, BUB1, GTSE1, HJURP, CDCA3, JPT1, CDC20, TTK, CDC25C, KIF2C, DLGAP5, CDCA2, CDCA8, ECT2, HMMR, AURKA, ANLN, CENPE, NEK2, GAS2L3, CENPA, not searching for symbol synonyms ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(pbmc[[c("S.Score", "G2M.Score", "Phase")]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

We don't regress anything out in this vignette. # Linear dimensional reduction - PCA Each cell is described by thousands of genes, which is too many dimensions to compare cells reliably. PCA compresses the variable genes into a small number of principal components (PCs) that capture the main axes of variation between cells. This also reduces noise: the sparse, noisy signal is averaged across correlated genes, so the top PCs mostly carry biological signal and the later ones mostly carry noise. The PCs, not the raw genes, are the input for the next steps: the nearest-neighbor graph, clustering and UMAP. The number of PCs we keep affects the results, and we usually choose it from an elbow plot. **How is it different from DESeq2?** - In a DESeq2 workflow, PCA is a quality-control and visualization step. It is calculated on transformed counts (variance-stabilized or rlog) and shows whether samples group by condition or batch, and whether there are outliers. - It is not used in the statistical test. Differential expression is tested for each gene with a negative binomial model, and the PCs are not an input. - With a handful of samples, you just look at the first two PCs, and you don't have to overcome the extensive technical noise in any single feature for scRNA-seq data, Seurat clusters cells based on their PCA scores, with each PC essentially representing a ‘metafeature’ that combines information across a correlated feature set. The top principal components therefore represent a robust compression of the dataset. However, how many components should we choose to include? 10? 20? 100? We can use elbow plot - a ranking of principle components based on the percentage of variance explained by each one ([`ElbowPlot()`](https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/elbowplot) function). In this example, we can observe an ‘elbow’ around PC9-10, suggesting that the majority of true signal is captured in the first 10 PCs. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ElbowPlot(pbmc) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_pbmc_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){fig-align='center' width=720} ::: ::: Choosing the optimal number of dimensions to use for downstream analyses can be challenging. If you are uncertain, it is better no include more PCs beyond the elbow, e.g 12-15. Cutting out the PCs, that don't contribute to explaining more variance, reduces the technical noise and can improve clustering. However, if your dataset contains rare cell type, that you wish to identify, you might need to include more dimensions, as rare cell types are often correlated with later PCs and might be barely distinguishable from the noise. Depending on what you try to discover, you may need to repeat downstream analyses with different number of PCs. In this tutorial we will use the first 10 PCs for downstream analyses. # Clustering The goal of clustering is to group cells with similar expression profiles, with the hope that each group corresponds to a cell type or state. Clustering is unsupervised: we don't tell the algorithm which cell types exist, we only look for structure in the data. Conceptually, Seurat does it in two steps: 1. **Build a graph of similar cells.** Each cell is connected to its nearest neighbors in PCA space (`FindNeighbors()`). Cells of the same type are close to each other, so they end up densely connected. 2. **Find communities in the graph.** An algorithm (Louvain by default, in `FindClusters()`) searches for groups of cells that are more connected to each other than to the rest. Each group is a cluster. The step is based on the PCs, not on all genes, so the number of PCs we selected earlier affects the clusters. The most important parameter is the **resolution**: a higher value gives more, smaller clusters, and a lower value gives fewer, larger clusters. There is no single correct value. Clusters are a way of splitting a continuous landscape of cells, and the right level of detail depends on your question. Common values are 0.4-1.2, and a good practice is to try a few and check whether the clusters make biological sense (do they have distinct marker genes?). Clusters that are not distinguishable by marker genes are probably over-split and can be merged. Keep in mind that clusters are not the same as cell types. They become cell types only after we annotate them using marker genes and prior knowledge. Also, the cluster numbers are arbitrary labels, and they can change if you rerun the analysis with different parameters. The default clustering method is Louvain, but we will use Leiden, as it slightly improves Louvain. In practice, on simple datasets like pbmc, these two clustering methods yield very similar results. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- FindNeighbors(pbmc, dims = 1:10) # here we use the number of PCs we wish to keep ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Computing nearest neighbor graph ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Computing SNN ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- FindClusters(pbmc, resolution = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1, 1.2), # we will try multiple resolutions algorithm = 4) # 4 = Leiden algorithm ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An object of class Seurat 11139 features across 2596 samples within 1 assay Active assay: RNA (11139 features, 2000 variable features) 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data 1 dimensional reduction calculated: pca ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Nearest neighbors info is stored here pbmc@graphs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $RNA_nn A Graph object containing 2596 cells $RNA_snn A Graph object containing 2596 cells ``` ::: ::: After running `FindClusters()`, there is a new column for each clustering resolution. **`RNA_snn_res.0.2`, `RNA_snn_res.0.5`**, **`RNA_snn_res.0.8`**, **`RNA_snn_res.1`**, **`RNA_snn_res.1.2`** and `seurat_clusters` which represents the last resolution that was run (1.2). ````` ::: ::: # Non-linear dimensional reduction - UMAP **Why not stop at PCA?** PCA is linear, and the first two PCs capture only a small part of the variation in single-cell data. Plotting PC1 vs PC2 usually shows overlapping populations, even if the cells are well separated in the 10-30 PCs we use for clustering. Non-linear methods (UMAP, t-SNE) compress this high-dimensional structure into 2 dimensions, so that we can see the clusters. They are used to visualize the data, and the clustering is not done on them. **Comparison with DESeq2:** in a DESeq2 workflow, the first two PCs are usually enough to see the few samples, so there is no need for a non-linear method. With thousands of cells, PC1 vs PC2 is not enough. **UMAP vs t-SNE** - Both place similar cells close together in 2D. - UMAP is faster, and it preserves more of the global structure (the relationships between clusters) than t-SNE, which mostly preserves local neighborhoods. - This is why UMAP is preferred, and it is the standard now. **Limitations: how not to overinterpret UMAP** - Distances are only meaningful locally. The distance between clusters and the size or density of clusters on the plot do not reflect the real distances or the number of cells. - Clusters that are close on the UMAP are not necessarily more similar, and the global layout can change between runs and parameters. - Continuous trajectories and gaps can be artifacts, as the method may tear or stretch the data. - The shape depends on parameters (e.g. the number of PCs and neighbors) and on the random seed. - Use UMAP for visualization and to check the clusters, not as evidence on its own. There is no single correct resolution. Clusters are a mathematical representation of the data, and the "right" number depends on the question you ask: a lower resolution for broad cell types (T cells, B cells, monocytes), a higher one to resolve subtypes (CD4 vs CD8 T cells). It is common to start coarse and sub-cluster only the populations of interest. **Considerations** - **Biological question:** how fine do you need to go? Do not split further than your question requires. - **Data size and complexity:** larger datasets with more cell types usually support higher resolutions. - **Over-clustering:** splits with no distinguishing genes, or clusters defined only by QC metrics, cell cycle or batch, are not worth keeping. - **Under-clustering:** distinct populations (e.g. a clear marker-defined group) that are merged into one cluster. - **Reproducibility:** the clustering depends on the number of PCs, the number of neighbors and the random seed, so check that your conclusions hold when these change slightly. **Techniques** - **Visual inspection:** color the UMAP by several resolutions (`DimPlot(pbmc, group.by = cl_names)`). - **Clustering tree:** the `clustree` package shows how cells from each cluster split when the resolution increases. Prefer a resolution where clusters have a single parent. Many crossing arrows mean an unstable clustering. - **Marker genes:** run `FindAllMarkers()` and check whether neighboring clusters have distinct markers. If two clusters have no clear markers separating them, merge them by choosing a lower resolution. - **Silhouette score:** measures how well each cell fits its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster (see `cluster::silhouette()` on the PCA embedding). Higher is better, but it favors a small number of clusters, so use it as a guide. - **Stability (bootstrapping):** re-cluster on subsets of cells or with different seeds and measure how often the same cells end up together (e.g. the `scclusteval` or `chooseR` approaches). Stable clusters are more trustworthy. ## Clustering tree Let's inspect the clustering tree ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} clustree(pbmc, prefix = "leiden_") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_pbmc_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-49-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: Each row is one resolution (top to bottom: 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2). - New clusters that add a new block: a resolution step is worth it if the extra cluster has its own markers (e.g. DCs at 0.8). - Persistence: splits that hold across several resolutions (confirm with clustree). **Overclustering:** - A new cluster’s genes are a subset of its sibling’s, or the same genes shared with its neighbors, just graded. - Top markers are MALAT1, ribosomal (RPS/RPL), mitochondrial or stress genes: a QC or state artifact, not a cell type. - Blurry diagonal, with blocks that bleed into neighbors. - Tiny clusters with no markers, or whose markers are low-expression and sparse. **Rule of thumb** - Resolution heavy depends on what you are trying to find. If you only care about main lineages (for example T cells, B cells) because later on you will focus on only one, it's completely fine to use small resolutions. If you want to identify subtypes of e.g. T cells, you need to increase the resolution. If you want to identify rare cell types you might even want to slightly overcluster and merge similar clusters later. - In my opinion, if you're not sure it is better to slightly overcluster than undercluster. **Leiden 0.2**: When we look at the clustering tree, we see that 0.2 –\> 0.5 cleanly splits almost each cluster in 2. Annotation means assigning a cell type or state to each cluster, so that we can interpret the results biologically. Annotation depends on the resolution we chose, so it should come after we have settled on one. It is one of the most important steps in single-cell analysis. Correct annotation allows for discovery of new biology and dictates all post-hoc analyses. Incorrect cell type annotation might lead to wrong or misleading conclusions. There are many ways to annotate clusters. The most common approaches are: - **Manual, marker-based:** compare the top markers of each cluster (from `FindAllMarkers()`) with known cell type markers from the literature or from databases such as PanglaoDB and CellMarker. This is what we did informally above (e.g. GNLY for NK cells, and so on). - **Manual, canonical marker-based**. Sometimes there are well known marker genes for certain cell types that didn't show up as top markers using marker detection. Sometimes depending on sequencing depth and other technical variables, canonical marker genes might not be detected at sufficient levels. - **Automated, reference-based:** transfer labels from an already annotated dataset, using tools such as `SingleR`, `Azimuth` or `CellTypist`. It is faster and more reproducible, but it can only label cell types that are present in the reference, and the labels depend on the quality of that reference. In practice, we use a combination of all these approaches, depending on the data, our prior expertise. Intersecting multiple methods gives us a higher confidence that our cluster represent true cell types. Things to keep in mind: - **Use several markers per cell type.** A single gene can be expressed in more than one cell type. - **Clusters can be mixed.** If a cluster contains two lineages, consider a higher resolution or sub-clustering it. - **Clusters can be technical.** A cluster without a clear cell type, with low-quality markers (e.g. `MALAT1`, ribosomal genes) or high mitochondrial content, may be a QC artifact and not a real population. - **Labels are hypotheses.** Annotations should be revisited when we learn more. > **Exercise 2** > > This is a pbmc dataset, so we know what cell types to expect in this experiment. > Find out what these cell types are and what their canonical marker genes are. > Use google, publications and public databases ([CellMarker 2](http://www.bio-bigdata.center/), [PanglaoDB](https://panglaodb.se/index.html), [CellGuide](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/cellguide)). > Use `FeaturePlot()` to confirm that the markers you found are detected and can represent a cell type. > Make a table: > > | Cell type | Proportion | Canonical markers | Cluster(s) | > |-----------|------------|-------------------|------------| > | | | | | > | | | | | > | | | | | > | | | | | > | | | | | > **Exercise 3** > > Take a look at the heatmap of top marker genes. > For each cluster, look up its top marker genes. > What cell type can marker each represent?
